title: A weakly etale universal homeomorphism is an isomorphism
statement:
Let $f:V\to W$ be a
weakly etale morphism
and a universal homeomorphism.
Then $f$ is an isomorphism.
(Source: [Stacks, Tag 0F6V](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0F6V).)

note: *Recorded in advance* from chapter *The trace formula* of the source.

proof.text: Put $P=V\times_WV$ and let $\delta:V\to P$ be the diagonal. By the definition of weakly etale, both $f$ and $\delta$ are flat. Every base change of $f$ is a homeomorphism, hence injective, so $f$ is universally injective by definition; taking the identity base change also shows that $f$ is surjective.

The homeomorphism underlying $f$ has image all of $W$, a closed subset, so [lem-trf-closed-embedding-affine] makes $f$ affine. Clause (3) of [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence] makes $f$ separated and quasi-compact. By the definition of separated, $\delta$ is a closed immersion. By the equivalence in [def-weil-radicial-morphism], universal injectivity of $f$ makes $\delta$ surjective.

source.place: Tag 0F6V, first two sentences of the proof; Morphisms Tags 04DE (lemma-homeomorphism-affine), 01S7 (lemma-affine-separated), 01S4 (lemma-universally-injective)

proof.text: The closed immersion $\delta$ is affine by clause (b) of [lem-weil-pbc-closed-immersion-integral-separated-uc], and hence quasi-compact by clause (3) of [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-permanence]. Thus $\delta$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact. It is also a monomorphism: if $a,b:T\to V$ satisfy $\delta a=\delta b$, composing with the first projection $P\to V$ gives $a=b$.

source.place: Tag 01S7, lemma-affine-separated; affine property of closed immersions; elementary diagonal identity from the fibre product

proof.text: Here is the elementary pullback argument used twice below. For any monomorphism $g:A\to B$ (meaning that $ga=gb$ implies $a=b$ for all scheme morphisms $a,b:T\to A$), let $q_1,q_2:A\times_BA\to A$ be the projections. The equality $gq_1=gq_2$ and monicity give $q_1=q_2$. The diagonal $d:A\to A\times_BA$ satisfies $q_1d=1_A$ and $dq_1=1_{A\times_BA}$, the latter because both sides have the same two projections. Thus both $q_1$ and $q_2=q_1$ are isomorphisms. The second projection $q_2:A\times_BA\to A$ is the base change of $g$ along itself, with the second copy of $A$ as the new base.

source.place: Tag 01L3, lemma-monomorphism: the categorical fibre-product argument, written out

proof.text: Apply step 4 to the monomorphism $\delta$. Its base change along itself is an isomorphism. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-isomorphism] with $h=\varphi=\delta$: step 3 verifies that this covering morphism is flat, surjective and quasi-compact, and step 4 verifies that the pulled-back morphism is an isomorphism. Therefore $\delta$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 02L4, lemma-descending-property-isomorphism; Tag 06NC, lemma-flat-surjective-quasi-compact-monomorphism-isomorphism, applied to the diagonal

proof.text: The isomorphism $\delta$ makes $f$ a monomorphism, as follows directly from the fibre product: if $a,b:T\to V$ satisfy $fa=fb$, their pairing $c=(a,b):T\to P$ factors as $\delta(\delta^{-1}c)$. Projecting this equality to the first and second factors gives $a=\delta^{-1}c=b$.

source.place: Tag 01L3, lemma-monomorphism, the converse implication written out

proof.text: Apply step 4 again, now to $f$, to see that the base change of $f$ along itself is an isomorphism. By steps 1 and 2, $f$ is flat, surjective and quasi-compact. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-fpqc-descend-isomorphism] with $h=\varphi=f$. It follows that $f$ is an isomorphism, as claimed.

proof_origin.place: Tag 0F6V, lemma-weakly-etale-universal-homeomorphism; flat surjective closed immersion proved using the existing fpqc descent node (02L4) and the explicit monomorphism calculation of 06NC

blueprint_update.statement:
Let $f:V\to W$ be a
weakly etale morphism
and a universal homeomorphism.
Then $f$ is an isomorphism.

proof.text:
By [def-weil-scheme-morphism-properties], $f$ is integral,
surjective and universally injective, and both $f$ and its diagonal
are flat. The diagonal is a closed immersion, since an integral map is
separated; it is surjective on underlying points by universal
injectivity. A flat surjective closed immersion is an isomorphism.
Indeed, on affines its ring map is $R\to R/I$, where $I$ is a nil
ideal and $R/I$ is flat. Tensoring the injection $(x)\to R$ with
$R/I$, for $x\in I$, gives $(x)/I(x)=0$; hence $x=ax$ for some
$a\in I$. Since $a$ is nilpotent, $1-a$ is a unit and $x=0$.
Thus $I=0$.

The diagonal of $f$ is therefore an isomorphism, so $f$ is a
monomorphism. On an affine open of $W$, integrality makes its
inverse image affine. The resulting ring map $R\to B$ is faithfully
flat and multiplication $B\otimes_R B\to B$ is an isomorphism.
The faithfully flat equalizer
$R\to B\rightrightarrows B\otimes_R B$ identifies $R$ with all of
$B$, because the two arrows both become the identity under
multiplication. Hence $R\to B$ is an isomorphism. These affine
identifications prove the assertion.
